The information I gave is based upon the statement of my deputy, who has seen the weighing actually going on, and the department is always careful to see that the coal is weighed.

I see two items, Geo. T. Davy, hauling up, wintering and launching the ' Speedy,' and on the same page an account of Geo. Summerville, wintering vessel, $75.
t Mr. PUGSLEY. That would not be the ' Speedy,' it might have been a caretaker, but I could not give the information tonight.
Are any of these items bought by public competition?
No, they are all bought by seeing different dealers, and getting the lowest prices.
I see a whistle, $65.
It is usual for steamers to have whistles, that is a fair price.

Has my hon. friend abolished the patronage list? Some ministers state that there has been a brand new departure lately, and that the patronage list is unknown. Would my hon. friend say that the list is unknown in his department?

Yes, I think I can safely say that the patronage list, as it used to exist from 30 to 40 years ago, down to last year, has been abolished. We do not furnish to our officials a list, as used to be done when my hon. friend, perhaps, had a good deal to do with patronage.
No.

Well, my hon. friend's predecessors in love and affection. We instruct our officials to buy where they get the goods cheapest, but I take it for granted, where there are articles of any considerable amount to be purchased, they will invite tenders. Where purchases are made through the department, the rule is that we invite tenders here, but the resident engineers, the superintendents of dredging, must buy supplies, and their instructions are to purchase them at reasonable prices.
When did the change take place1?
It was announced last session, I think.
Does the minister find, under the new arrangement, that goods have been purchased cheaper?

I do not think so, not so far as ordinary supplies are concerned. There has been a difference and a saving to the department in this respect, that when we require fittings for different public buildings we are in the habit of giving a wider advertisement than was formerly the case. We secure greater competition, and I think the accounts will show that we are making a considerable saving in that way.
Would the minister state that within the last year there has been really any change in the list of firms from whom the department has been purchasing?

I do not follow that at all. Having done away with the patronage list, it is no part of my duty to follow that. We leave that to the discretion and judgment of our buyers and do not interfere with them at all.
Does the hon. minister say that the agents of his department have full liberty to purchase goods from any one outside the supporters of the government?
They have a perfectly free hand.
It is strange then that they do not seem to make use of their freedom.
They would lose their job if they did.
No, I never inquire from whom they buy.
My hon. friend says that where tenders are called for, he has broadened the scope of the advertisement. Does he now advertise in any newspapers other than those supporting the government?

No, we have not ordinarily found it necessary to do so. We can get sufficiently wide publicity by utilizing the papers friendly to the government. What I meant was that we have widened the circle in the way of informing contractors. Formerly the practice was not to advertise in the newspapers for fittings but to send out to people in the business asking them to tender. We now, however, advertise generally in the newspapers so that there is wider competition and the same opportunity is given to Conservatives as to Liberals.
But the hon. minister does not deem it expedient to advertise in any Conservative newspapers?
We have not found it necessary to do that.

Where the hon. minister finds a Conservative newspaper in a city
having a very much larger circulation than the newspaper supporting my hon. friend's government, he will still advertise in the newspaper with the smaller circulation, and not in the Conservative newspaper with a much larger circulation. He will have some difficulty in explaining that there is very much change in this practice from the former one. The only difference he says is that heretofore the department had a list and only invited the people on the list to tender for supplies, but that now he has broadened that practice by advertising in the newspapers which support the government. Does my hon. friend think that is a change in the public interest?
I think so.
Would not that rather increase the government patronage?
No.

I beg to differ with my hon. friend on that point. Heretofore he had a list of the faithful, but now he advertises in the newspapers that support the government but not in any other. How does he know that a paper supports the government or not? Has he a list of the papers supporting the government?
As a rule, I endeavour to see if they take an enlightened view of public matters. From that I can pretty well judge on what side they are.

The minister appears to think that in the letting of contracts for supplies he is taking an entirely new departure and is giving Conservatives just as good an opportunity to tender as Liberals. But he knows that the Conservatives, to a large extent, do not take Liberal papers.
That is a great misfortune. I am surprised at that.

When it comes down to advertising for tenders, it does not seem very good practice for the minister to advertise only in government newspapers. If he were conducting his own business, he would not conduct it in that way.

My hon. friend the minister read out a few items a moment ago which he said were fair and reasonable. Let me draw a few to his attention, taken from page V-319 of the Auditor General's Report. On dredge scows- Mr. Davie had something to do with this -he spent $1,333.13. Let me just mention a few items and ask the hon. gentleman if he considers the prices fair. Elm, 950 feet at 8 cents per foot or $80 per 1,000 feet. Why, we are buying elm lumoer at home at $12 per 1,000 feet.
Where?
At my home.
That must be an elm country. Is that what they call swamp elm?
What my hon. friend bought no doubt was slippery elm.
I would sooner have that than swamp elm. My hon. friend will not answer my question.
Here is an item of iron spikes, 457 pounds at 6 cents per pound. I want my hon. friend to state if 6 cents for spikes is a fair price. He can buy them by retail at 3 cents.
The chief engineer disputes that statement absolutely.
Let him go to any hardware store and he will get them at 3 cents per pound. What do you pay for railway spikes on the Intercolonial Railway?
There is a vast difference in spikes.
You buy them by the ton for the railway.
There is a difference between ship spikes and iron spikes.
They are all made of iron and steel, and steel and iron are the same price to-day.
I am told not.
I know better, for I am handling 1,000 tons every year. Here is an item for labour, one and a half day at $5 per day.
It depends on whether that was expert labour or not.
$5 a day would be a pretty good price for Mr. Davie himself.
Ship spikes and steel spikes are entirely different. Ship spikes are wrought spikes. They are entirely different from the ordinary wire spikes and cut spikes.
Here is oakum, 434 pounds at 8 cents per pound. What is pitch worth a barrel?
I do not know. I never handled it. We do not use it.
It is used in Kingston. The government use a good deal and pay $5.50. I can buy it at $3.50 laid down.
How many barrels are charged there?
Four. The government are paying $5.50, and other people can buy it for repairing their roofs at $3.50. Then, there is an item, use of forges, etc.,

$30. These are hand forges that you can buy at $15 or $16 apiece. Yet, the department pays $30 for the use of two or three of them. Another item reads, use of tools, $75. These are tools brought over to repair these scows. And the minister pays a bill like that. It is like the cross-cut saw that was spoken of last year for the use of which $30 was paid. Then there is cartage of tools, etc., to and from dock, $25. Also wood wedges, $25.60. I am sure that if we moved for these accounts and got them down, we should find them all certified as ' fair and just '. But plenty of the members on that side of the House know that the prices of some of these articles are not fair and just. And the minister pays these prices that are made without tender and without calling for competition. Then he will tell us that the patronage list is done away with.

The hon. member (Mr. George Taylor) is out, as he sometimes-I will not say always-is. Take, for instance, the item of $5 for labour about which he makes such an outcry. This is a day and a half at $5 for the day and a half.
No, it is carried out at $7.50.
Well, I will not quarrel with my hon. friend over $2.50. With regard to the elm, I am told that such elm as was used for this work costs what is charged. It is what they call rock elm.
You can buy it for $20 a thousand.
The hon. member said it could be bought for $12.
I say we are buying it at $12-not rock elm.
I think we should be glad to take all that the hon. member (Mr. George Taylor) can furnish at a good deal more than $20. With regard to the hire of tools-	i
I will say that if the rock elm is of the right kind it is worth $80 a thousand.
I presume my hon. friend (Mr. Nesbitt) is a good judge of it.
Yes, I know all about it. I will guarantee that I know more about it than Die hon. member (Mr. George Tay-lar), and put up money on it.
I dont' bet money.
My hon. friend ought to be fair. You cannot buy mill run rock elm with the culls out, for $20.
It does me good to have a practical man meet my hon. friend (Mr. George Taylor)-

I do not admit that the hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) is a practical man-practising law and knowing all about the price of lumber. I will tell him that we can buy elm lumber-we refuse it-at $12 a thousand, and not mill run-

I do not believe there is a man in the world who would be foolish enough to sell mill run, culls out, rock elm at $20 a thousand. And even swamp elm cannot be bought at $12 a thousand, unless he takes it mill run without the culls out.
We are buying it, cut, four, five and six inches, specially sawn, five-eights thick, at $12 a thousand.
Log run?
No. I know what we are doing.

From what the chief engineer of my department tells me-and he is an expert, buying these materials continually-I am led to believe that my hon. friend from North Oxford is a much more practical man than the hon. member opposite (Mr. Geo. Taylor).
On what does the minister base his judgment?
On the opinion given me by a gentleman who knows about these prices.
I thought it was on the noise the hon. gentleman made.
I have a letter upstairs offering me $18 a thousand, log run, dead culls out, for swamp elm.
Is that from the government?
No, from a private party.
Carried.
No, the minister was about to explain about the tools.
This was in cases where the work was done by our own men.
How about the $30 for a couple of hand forges?
It depends on how long they were used.
You can buy them for $15 a piece.
What is the difference between the maintenance expenses and operating expenses as shown in the return brought down to the motion of the hon. member for Welland (Mr. German)?

It is sometimes difficult to draw the line between the two. In operating expenses are included wages, coal, oil and other items of that kind. Some
slight repairs might also be charged in operating expenses. But it is at this point that it is hard to draw the line.
What principle does the department follow?
The chief engineer tells me that there are charged to maintenance, those repairs which cannot be fairly made, by the crew when the boat is in use.
Are the expenses of each of these dredges shown separately in the Auditor General's Report-all the ex-: penses of each dredge?
I understand so.

In the case of the dredge ' Challenge,' I find at page V-305 of the renort of the Auditor General for the* year 1908-9, the items chargeable against the vote amounted to $7,394.44. But in the return brought down, the operating and maintenance expenses amount to $12,058.27. Why do not the items in the Auditor General's Report and in this return correspond?

The reason might be this:	The statement in V-305, I think, is
for dredge vessel repairs. In the statement which the department brings down, there is the cost of operating, $5,976 and the cost of maintenance, $6,081. Now the Auditor General may not apportion the cost of dredge vessel repairs or of operating and maintenance the same as the department does, he may take a different view. But the total should be the same for the 1 Challenge.' The two items, dredge vessel repairs and dredging, ought together to make the sum total we have in our re turn. But the difference would be accounted for by the fact that the auditor might take a different view of the operating expenses.
I understand that the expenditure chargeable against any dredge, both for operating and maintenance, would be included under the name of the dredge in the report.
No, because there is another item for dredging. My hon. friend will see in the estimates, page 72, for Quebec and Ontario, dredging, which includes operating expenses.

Is there any account kept with regard to this dredging work, giving the cost of dredging, then what amount of material the dredge has taken out, so as to get an idea of what the dredge is doing in the shape of work per day, and per quantity, classifying the cost, and ascertaining how much that class of work is costing?

That is done periodically. My hon. friend will find all that

in the annual report of the department. The report does not write off anything for depreciation, but the actual cost of operating is given with the quantity of dredging.
Dredging plant, Manitoba, $13,000.

This amount is to make provision for the construction of new dredging plant to do the dredging required in Manitoba. We require a new hull and boiler and a small tug for the dredge 'Assiniboine'; also a new hull for the dredge crane, and improvements in machinery.
Where is that dredge going to operate?
The 'Assiniboine' works at the mouth of the Red river near Selkirk.
Is thaj, the new dredge built last year, constructed out of an old snag boat?
I think the 'Assiniboine ' was renewed about a year and a half ago.
The dredge I refer to was a snag boat converted into ai dredge. I understand they are both working at the mouth of the Red river. One was a suction dredge, and the other a dipper dredge.

I am not familiar with the names of the dredges, but the chief engineer tells me the 'Assiniboine' is working at the mouth of the Red river.
Dredging plant, Saskatchewan and Alberta, $65,000.

This is to make- provision for building two snag boats and stone lifters, to be operated on the Saskatchewan river. We find these boats are urgently required to remove boulders and improve the navigation of the river.
Dredging plant, British Columbia, $160,000.

A new elevator dredge is required, and we require a gasoline launch for use on the Thomson raver by the assistant resident engineer estimated to oost $5,000. Then we want a drilling plant for Victoria harbour, $30,000. We shall have to increase this vote largely. Improvements are very urgently required in Victoria harbour, and we want to make them more rapidly. These improvements are required by reason of the Grand Trunk Pacific having determined to build a wharf in Victoria harbour. They have applied to the department for approval of the location of it, and it is going to very seriously interfere with other steamers coming in unless we can widen the harbour. We will find it neees-Mr. PUGSLEY.
sary to do a considerable amount of rock blasting and also a considerable amount of dredging. We have now in contemplation the purchasing of two Lobnitz rock breakers. We propose operating both of them and also having double shifts in order to get through with the work as rapidly as we can. The work is most urgently needed by reason of the increased number of steamers that are going to Victoria harbour. There are steamers running between Seattle and Victoria, between Vancouver and Victoria, between Prince Rupert and Victoria, and the number is to be supplemented by the steamers that have lately been acquired by the Grand Trunk Pacific. Therefore, we shall have to ask probably a little later on for a considerable increase in this vote. Then, in regard^ also to Vancouver harbour, we shall require a very considerable increase. We have had a very careful survey made of the entrance to Vancouver harbour, or what is known as the first narrows, and we propose to do a very important and very necessary work in the immediate future, namely: the widening of the channel to about 1,200 feet. This work is going to cost up probably $400,00, apart from the cost of the dredge. We will require a dredge having peculiar features to do that work most expeditiously and economically. The dredge which the engineer recommends is one of the elevator variety.
Is that the dredge you referred to?
Yes, and that dredge, it is estimated, will cost somewhere in the vicinity of $275,000 in addition to the duty.
Why could not that he built in Canada?

The only dredge of the kind that has ever been built in Canada is the ' Fielding,' which was built at the Sorel shipyards, and which cost very considerably more money than this dredge cost. We may be able to get it built in Canada although it would take considerable time. This work is urgent. We have not positively decided that we shall go abroad. If we can get it built in Canada within the time that we ought to have it at work we shall be very glad to do so.
I understand the minister to say that the elevator dredge for which $135,000 of this item is intended is for work on the first narrows?
Yes.
That is the dredge the minister is speaking about?
Yes.

As I understand from the reports of the various engineers who have

examined the situation, an ordinary dipper dredge or a suction dredge will not do; it must be an elevator dredge. Did I understand the minister to say that dredge will be ordered in Canada or not?

No. what I said was that I am inclined to think that we shall find it most advantageous to purchase that dredge in the old country, because these dredges are not ordinarily built in Canada.
I do not know of any elevator dredge built in Canada except the ' Fielding/ The capacity of the ' Fielding/ is about the same as the dredge we propose buying, and if I am right in the figures we will get this dredge, which is of steel and has a capacity of about 800 or 1,000 cubic yards per hour, for about half the cost of the ' Fielding,' excluding the duty. If upon inquiry we find that we can get an elevator dredge built in Canada within a reasonable time, I would be very glad indeed to get it here, but I am sure we can get it very much earlier if we buy it abroad.
It is the advice of the government engineer, is it not, that it will be necessary, in order to get the right kind of dredge, to order it in the old country?
Yes, of the resident engineer.
Did I understand the minister to say that this item will have to be increased?
Yes.
I understand then that the $90,000 taken out of this item will not be devoted to the purchase of a dredge or plant?
No, we will use the $90,000 for operating.
Might I ask the minister, who has been giving, I am very pleased to be able to say, good attention to the first narrows, about when the dredge will be ordered, and in operation?

The dredge will be ordered immediately upon the passing of the Appropriation Act. We have, no power to give an order till then, but immediately after the Appropriation Act passes we shall give the order for the dredge. We are making inquiries and getting all the information, but we cannot enter into a contract until the Appropriation Act passes. I recognize the great importance of going on at the earliest possible moment with this work of widening the first narrows, and also the work in Victoria harbour. The work at both places is most urgently required, and I can assure my hon. friends from British Columbia, that there will be no time lost whatever after the Appropriation Act is pessed.
I think the minister is aware that on the south side of the narrows there are some submerged or partly submerged rocks that the engineer advises should be removed?
Yes.
Some 63,000 yards, I believe. May I ask the minister what machinery is being provided for the removal of that rock?
That will be removed by means of the Lobnitz rock crusher. We also propose to remove the Parthia shoals as well.
That is one of the objects for which these rock crushers are to be purchased?

Yes, we intend using Lobnitz rock crushers there, and at Victoria harbour. We will put them at work in Victoria harbour first, but we will start work at the first narrows as soon as we can conveniently, and we will use the Lobnitz crushers on the south side of the channel.

I think the attention of the minister was drawn when he was_ at Vancouver to the necessity of providing anchorage for vessels in English bay, at a cost for dredging and a breakwater of somewhere in the neighbourhood of $50,000.
I do not remember just what the cost is estimated to be, but I remember my attention being called^to the need of it.
May I ask the minister what provision is being made for that very much needed work?

We are taking an amount for operating the dredging plant in British Columbia. We have several very urgent propositions in British Columbia in respect to dredging. We have the Fraser river, the north arm of the Fraser, the entrance to False creek, the Vancouver Narrows, Victoria harbour, and Nanaimo. These are the most important places. Then we have quite a number of less important harbours in British Columbia where dredging work i3 urgently required. All I can say to my hon. friend to-night is that we shall give attention to the work of dredging the basin at the entrance to False creek as soon as we can, but I feel that the first * work to be done is the widening of the narrows.
The present estimates make no provision for that?
Not specially for the work at the entrance to False creek. It can be done out of the general vote, if we have enough money.
I understood that the engineer suggested that there should be a breakwater as well as a little dredging at the entrance to False creek.

We would require a special vote for that. I did not understand that a breakwater was needed, but simply dredging of a basin, and the approach to provide an anchoring ground for vessels entering False creek.
Do the estimates before the House provide for the removal of Par-thia shoal? I think the minister is aware that that will not require a rock cutter, but only an ordinary dredge.

Yes. Both the widening of the narrows and the removal of Parthia shoal could be done out of the general
dredging vote.

The minister, with a keen eye to the situation, notwithstanding the entertainment he received at Vancouver, was good enough to tell us that we would have a dredge before the season expired. Our seasons there are fairly long, like our patience. We would be glad if the minister would be good enough to say, if he can, when a dredge for this general work is likely to be in the harbour.

From the best information I can get, I believe we can have an elevator dredge launched by the middle or latter part of July, and we can have her at work in Vancouver harbour probably bv the first of September.

I was referring, not to the elevator dredge, but to the ordinary dipper dredge, which has a good deal of work to do there-the removal of Parthia shoal, for instance. I believe that the engineer has recommended very strongly that a dredge should be got there at once to do this work.

I may say to my hon. friend that the dredges are all busy. The ' King Edward ' is, I think, at this very moment engaged in dredging in False creek at the request of the city of Vancouver. We brought her from Nanaimo for the very purpose of doing urgent work there. What we are trying to do is to keep all the dredges busy all the time. I can assure my hon. friend that the removal of Parthia shoal will be done just as soon as we can do it.
I did not quite catch what the minister said about $5,000 for a launch.
That is applied for by Mr. Aylmer, the resident engineer, for use on the Thompson river.
What work is he doing on the Thompson river?

There is work all around there-east and west, north and south; for instance, the inspection of booms, and the clearing out of the channel. Then, the Thompson river connects with the Shus-wap lakes, and his duties will take him there. He told me when I was in British Columbia last year that he could not do his work without having a launch for the purpose of getting to these inland waters.
Is the engineer changing his headquarters from Revelstoke to Kamloops?
Yes.
The minister had an application for some dredging on the North Thompson river to make that navigable. Will that be part of the work?

Not out of this vote, but that work, if recommended by Mr. Aylmer, will have careful consideration. He thought Kamloops would be a more central point for him, in view of the duties he has to perform in various directions.

In regard to the rock drilling plants which the minister spoke of for the harbour of Victoria, about how soon does he expect to begin operations there?
Mr. PUGSLEi. We shall have to build very heavy scows on which the rock drilling plants are to be placed, and it will take probably three or four months to have the rock drilling plants delivered, as they are made in the old country. Of course, I cannot enter into a contract until the Appropriation Act passes.

It appears that this return does not comply with the order of the House, because it contains only a list of the dredges owned by the Department of Public Works. The return is indorsed as a return to an order of the House of Commons dated 15th March, 1909, showing the number and names of the various dredges owned by the government. This deals only with the dredges owned by the Public Works Department, and so does not comply with the order of the House.

It complies as far as my department is concerned. It would be for the Marine Department and the Railways and Canals Department to bring down their returns separately. This is limited to the Department of Public Works and professedly so. If my hon. friend would bring the matter to the notice of the other ministers, I have no doubt they would bring down their parts of the return.
Why should it be necessary for an hon. member to call the attention of the government further?

It may be that the member only wished the Public Works Depart-

ment dredges. -I know it was to me he spoke.

Referring to the first narrows works, what is the capacity of the elevating dredges, what is the quantity that it is estimated will have to be removed, and will the $90,000 be sufficient to carry on the work to the end of the year?

The quantity is estimated at about 2,500,000 yards, and the actual cost of removal with a powerful elevator dredge, without making any allowance for interest upon the cost of the dredge, wear and tear, sinking fund, &c., will probably be about 15 cents per cubic yard. The dredge has a capacity of aboujti 800 cubic yards per hour. There will be no question about keeping the work going when we get the drege there, it will be kept going.
New Dredging Plant, Generally, $340,000.
What is the lowest price per cubic yard for any dredging done! under the Dussault-Lemieux contract in Quebec harbour?
That is art entire contract for wharf building and dredging together. For dredging, my recollection is, it is 57 cents per cubic yard scow measurement for the crib seats.
When the minister rents a scow to a sub-contractor, I understand he rents the crew and outfit?
No, just the bare scow
A dredge?
If we rent a dredge, that includes the crew, because we have to keep our crew aboard.

So in 1908, when the Dredge ' International ' was rented to Dus-sault et Lemieux, we received $25,200 at 15 cents per cubic yard. That would be
168,000	cubic yards for which the contractor would receive 57 cents a cubic yard, and we, although we supplied the dredge and all the men, paid all the wages and bore the whole expense of the dredge, received only 15 cents a cubic yard. In other words, the contractor made 42 cents' a cubic yard, and on the item of rent of the dredge alone, he has a profit of something like $57,200. The resident engineer, Mr. Valiquette, stated before the Public Accounts Committee last year that while the department received $150 a day, the expenses and upkeep came to $125, leaving apparently a profit to the department of $25 a day, but it was shown by the evidence of the same witness, that sometimes as much as 1,000 cubic yards, amounting ot $800 or $900, was dredged, so the contractor was making $600 or $700 a day out of the dredge, and the department was making only $25. According to the
minister's statements, this item will give as alarming a profit out of a dredge owned and operated by the government
Which dredge is that?

The ' International.' The government pay all the expenses, and all they receive is 15 cents, and the department pays .the contractor 57 cents for the work we do with our own men and dredge, while we pay all the expenses. In other words, out of that contract the contractor is making $67,000.
The hon. gentleman is far from stating all of the facts in the case.
I have stated all the facts from the minister's answers.
He has overlooked some facts.
Then it is due to the minister's answers.

The hon. gentleman overlooked some things. The contract was made long before I became Minister of Public Works. I found it in operation when I became minister. The dredge ' International ' dredged out the crib seats, it is true, for the contractor, but it was also dredging out the channel, and, under ordinary circumstances, that dredged material would have been taken out three miles or so to deep water and dumped there. But the contractor, who had the contract for the crib work, dredging, and back filling- which he, being the lowest tenderer, obtained after public competition-bought this material from the government and paid 15 cents per cubic yard all round, not only for what was taken out of the crib seats, but also for vast quantities which the government was not paying him a copper for. The result, as brought out before the Public Accounts Committee, was that the government was actually the gainer by the operation.
I do not remember that.

The hon. member for Leeds (Mr. George Taylor) brought that question up a couple of years ago, but when he found out the facts he dropped it like a hot potato, and we heard nothing more about it until my hon. friend resurrected the matter to-night. When I became minister I found, in connection with the further work, that there would be a greater amount of dredging in connection with the crib seats and less channel work, and I saw the thing would not work out as before. These contractors were going on with the work of building the cribs in regard to which their tender was very low-much less than the work could be done for to-day, in view of the advances in prices of materials. I made a new bargain and insisted on their

paying $200 per day for the use of the dredge. After allowing for the cost _ of operation and wear and tear, and sinking fund and a reasonable contractor's profit, that gives to the government for the dredge ' International ' $110 per day in profit.
How many cubic yards per day?
It varies from day to day. Some days she would strike hard material and dredge a less quantity, or storms might arise when she would be more or less idle.

The hon. minister's statement may be clear to himself, but I cannot understand it. The bare fact is this, that the dredge was rented by the contractor on a cubic yard basis at 15 cents per' yard and he is paid for excavation at the rate of 57 cents per yard, so that while the government dredge did the work the *contractor got a profit on that work of 42 cents per cubic yard.
That is not so.

The hon. minister obscures the issue by bringing in a lot of side contracts, dumping down the river, filling in the crib work, &c., but the main fact is that the dredge was rented by the contractor at 15 cents per cubic yard, and the contractor was paid 75 cents per cubic yard, and we did all the work, thus leaving him net 42 cents on our work.

That is not the case. That was ventilated before the Public Accounts Committee two years ago, and we never heard a word of it last session from my hon. friend or the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. George Taylor) when the matter was fresh in their memory. Now, however, when not only my hon. friend but others have forgotten the facts most absolutely essential to understand the matter, my hon. friend brings it up again. But in so doing he forgets the most essential fact, which is that, while we were paying for a portion of the dredging at 57 cents per cubic yard, the contractor was paying the government for thousands upon thousands of cubic yards for which he was not getting one cent from the government, so that the one account over-balanced the other, and the government received more than it paid out to the contractor. When I became minister I found that there was more dredging to be done in connection with the crib seats and less channel work, so I made the contractor pay $200 per day for the use of the dredge, on which we get a net profit of $110. There are many days when the dredge would not average 700 yards. It does not average that for the season. On some days, therefore, we would be getting at the rate of 40 or 50 cents per cubic yard for the work done.
When we lend a dredge at so much per cubic yard, if there be a day when the dredge is not working the government pays the inspection.
This charge is for every day, whether the dredge works or not.
I am not speaking of the $200 per day, but of the item per cubic yard.
That was an old arrangement before I was minister.
Perhaps the hon. gentleman will admit that I was correct so far as 1908 was concerned?

No, because my hon. friend leaves out of account the vast quantity of dredging out of the channel for which the contractor was not receiving one cent from the government, and which, if the arrangement had not been made with the contractor, we would have had to tow out to deep water some three or four miles distant. For those thousands and thousands of cubic yards of dredged material, the contractor paid us and used it for back filling.
If he had not got it from the government, he would have got it from some one else.
But we would have had to tow it out to sea and dump it there.
Does the $90 a day cover the wages of the crew and the expenses in connection with the dredging as well as interest upon the investment?
$91 covers the wages, the coal, the interest upon the expenditure, and a reasonable amount for wear and tear.
What is the capacity of the dredge?
Working under favourable circumstances, about 700 cubic yards per day at that depth of water.
What is the depth of water?

Forty-eight feet.
Dredging, maritime provinces, $675,000.
What are the details?

It is impossible to tell in a minute detail where this will be expended. We have many demands from different sections of the country. This covers the cost of operation of the government dredges in the maritime provinces, as well as contract work.
Has the minister an estimate which shows where the dredging is to be done?
All this next summer?
As far as we can get along.
I did not hear
And Gaspereau.

Ah, I was going to say that I had not heard the minister say anything of Gaspereau. I want to impress upon the minister the absolute necessity of the continuance of the work commenced there in 1908. He was not in the House at that time, and was not familiar with the circumstances, but as early as 1901, the Minister of Public Works of that day, the late Mr. Tarte, had the original survey made and items were put into the estimates for one or two years, encouraging the people there to believe that the work would be speedily prosecuted, but year after vear disappointment came. There are some very large industries there requiring navigation facilities. There are large lumbering operations, a canning establishment and others. Steamers go there and boats ply up and down the river. The difficulty in the way of navigation is the bar near the mouth of the river. The main reason always given for not going on with the work was that there were not dredging plants available-that the government had not dredges in the maritime provinces to undertake the work. In 1908 tenders were asked for and operations begun. In the spring of 1909-unfortunately, in my judgment, and to the injury of the work that had already been commenced in 1908-the work was not prosecuted. It was near the close of the season of 1909 when the government dredge was sent. Then, owing to the' inclemency of the weather, she had soon to desist from operations. The work done in 1908 would have been of advantage had the bar been completely dredged through so that the channel of the river could have been reached. But, unless this work is prosecuted so as to reach that channel every dollar that has been expended is absolutely wasted. I know the minister has made every effort to have this work done, and I can appreciate the fact that he has been besieged from every section of the maritime provinces for dredging. There is more work to be done than the plant can accomplish. I know that that has been the case ever since I first had any knowledge of thpse things-and my knowledge began in 1900, when I first became a member of this House. Still, I would strongly urge upon the department the continuance of the work this year. It seems to me it would not require a great deal more to make the work already done of practical advantage to the port and to the shippers who find it necessary to reach that port. Larger vessels are being used, and a great deal of lumber is being exported. As a result of the conditions of the channel, the lumber merchants are sending their lumber to Cape Tormentine and other ports, incurring the cost of railway charges, this being necessary in order to secure shipping facilities. If the dredging were completed vessels would go up the river and load at the wharfs of the lumber establishments at Port Elgin.
How far is Port Elgin from the mouth of the river?
I am not sure, but I should estimate it at between a mile and a mile and a half.
Who owns the wharf?
The lumber establishment own wharfs where they would ship if the vessels could reach them. Then there are fishing concerns, that ship.
Does the government own any wharf there?

I think there is an old landing wharf below the railway drawbridge. But the main shipping would be done at the wharfs above the draw-bridge. The New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island Railway which connects Sackville at the Intercolonial Junction with Cape Tormentine opposite Prince Edward Island, passes through Port Elgin and crosses the Gaspereau river at that point. In the bridge they have a draw to enable vessels to pass up and down the stream. Small vessels can go there. There is a large business with Prince Edward Island.
Do small vessels go to Port Elgin now?
Vessels with light draft-yes.
What draught?
They can go at high tide.

The difliculty is the bar which prevents the approach to the river. The river opens out into the Bay Verte. The sweep of the sea from Northumberland straits up into the bay has

formed this bar. In former days, I am told, larger vessels could approach that river and navigate these waters.
Would not the river require to be dredged?

Not to Port Elgin. After you get beyond a certain point the channel is sufficiently deep. The dredging is necessary at the mouth of the river -that is my understanding of it. The people there were very much interested. They have from time to time got up petitions and had public meetings. They are very anxious for the advancement of the trade of that section of New Brunswick, and so to have this work proceeded with. I cannot use language strong enough in which to urge upon the minister the importance and necessity of this work. I think he has had applications from time to time directly from the residents of that community, and must himself have some idea of the necessity of the work. He can readily understand, representing that constituency, and coming more closely in touch with the people, how zealous they are in approaching me, and if I could be inspired with the same zeal in my attempts to approach him, I am sure my appeal will be a successful one.

I have been very strongly urged by my hon. friend, repeatedly and incessantly urged, to complete this work. I have also been urged by prominent business men of Port Elgin, and I am happy to be able to say to my hon. friend that I anticipate that early in the coming season I shall be able to continue this work with one of the government dredges, probably the same one which was there last year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I wish to remind the Minister of Public Works that there are a number of places in Nova Scotia, which he has not mentioned, but for which I shall not fail to put in an application in due course, places in which my constituents are interested.
I thought that everybody was served in the county of the Finance Minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not at all. My hon. friend must come down and see that lovely neighbourhood.

I would like to ask the member for Westmorland (Mr. Emmer-son) if I correctly understood him to say that the government dredge was sent there too late in the season of 1909 to do any work, on account of stress of wreather.

I commenced early in the spring urging the minister to send a dredge there. His answer was that he Mr. EMMERSON.
hoped to have one available very shortly, one which was engaged either in Prince Edward Island or in Nova Scotia; he hoped that she would be relieved shortly and would go there early in the season. I assumed that it was because he was disappointed in his expectations that the dredge did not reach there earlier. She did reach there and did some work, but the season closed early with rough weather, and they were compelled to take her away.

Following up the item which has just been introduced by the hon. member for Westmorland, asking for an appropriation for government dredging in some of those minor streams, I would like to ask whether the local government in New Brunswick does not do a good deal of this kind of work.

No. I may say that the harbours and streams in the maritime provinces, as elsewhere in Canada, are not only under the control of the Dominion government, but are entirely within their jurisdiction. The provincial government and legislatures have never recognized any responsibility with regard to them for that reason, and for the further reason, that this dredging work being for the promotion of navigation, it is exclusively under the jurisdiction of the Dominion.
I might point out that in the province of Ontario a good deal of this kind of work has been done by the provincial government, on just such streams as the hon. gentleman has made a plea for.
In harbours?
Navigable streams.
The provincial government?
Yes, I have seen them doing it myself.
Would the hon. gentleman be good enough to tell me of any case where the Ontario government has done any dredging, except of course in connection with drainage works?

Yes, in the Muskoka rivers and Muskoka lakes, and I have seen them doing it. You will find them dredging below Huntsville, where they have worked in a chain of lakes and have made these lakes navigable for steamers. They have done dredging in Peninsula lake.
I must say that the provincial authorities of Ontario have shown a magnaminity which is refreshing.

I think they will be inclined to drop this kind of thing if the

Dominion government does it in other provinces.
I think the hon. gentleman will find that it has been pretty well dropped long ago.

I know a good deal of that work has been done in the upper lakes by the local government. I think it would he unfair to saddle this kind of work on one province and do it for other provinces. If that is the way it is viewed in the maritime provinces, I am pleased to know it. We will know where to go to get dredging done in future.

The Dominion government has done far more in the way of dredging for the province of Ontario than for any other province, I think we are doing more for Ontario than for all the other provinces combined. Take Port Arthur, Fort William, Victoria Harbour, Tiffin, Midland, Goderich, Port Burwell, Port Stanley, Eondeau, Cobourg, Toronto, Hamilton, Port Dalhousie-take them altogether, and you will find that they amount to as much as the dredging in all the other provinces put together. What my hon. friend says is a surprise to me. It is a strange thing that, having been minister for some years, I do not know of any dredging work being done by the government of the province of Ontario. I never heard of such a thing.
In the -very next item the maritime provinces get $675,000, a general vote for dredging, while Ontario and Quebec combined get the same amount. So the hon. gentleman is entirely wrong.
Go back to capital account, page 55, and you will find for Fort William and Port Arthur, $800,000, Tiffin, $120,000, Victoria Harbour, $145,000.

Has the minister estimated the cost of the work that will be necessary at Gaspereau to make a channel which will enable vessels to go up to Port Elgin, as suggested by the hon. member for Westmorland?
My recollection is that it is somewhere in the vicinity of 200,000 cubic yards.
Does that include dredging in the river as well as at the bar?
Yes. That will be dredging to give access to Port Elgin.

I do not propose to discuss this matter, because it has been under investigation in the Public Accounts Committee. But I saw the report of the resident engineer, Mr. Stephens, in which 152
he stated that the depth of water there varied from 8 inches to 5 or 6 feet. Perhaps the hon. member for Westmorland has some information.

On account of this bar a good deal of sawdust has floated down the stream and has reached a point between where the waters of the bay join with the waters of the river. There are some sawdust banks and they are a measureable obstruction, but they are of such a character that vessels going in and out, while they touch them are propelled or hauled through, I think, by tugs, and the passage is not difficult. As a result of that there may be a variation in the depth of the water near the mouth of the river. The cost of the removal of such obstruction would be a mere bagatelle. The main dredging is in connection with the bar and, where the bar comes along the channel, straightening the channel. '

Did I correctly understand, the minister to say that the dredging which was done in 1908 did not complete the channel through the bar, But that it was left in such a condition that if the work is not continued that which has already been done will fill up and there will be an absolute waste of money?
When it is completed through the bar the work will be done.

If you undertake to make a channel through a bar, only cut a certain distance of it, and do not complete the whole channel, and the channel is not available between the harbour and the sea outside, it follows that unless that work is prosecuted through, the money already expended will practically be made useless.
That is the condition in which the work was left in the fall of 1908?
Yes, that is the condition in which it was left in the fall of 1908. Unfortunately some heavy storms came there that compelled the removal of the dredge. It is a very difficult place to dredge.
Because of the class of material?

No, but because of the winds and the exposed position of the dredge. When the winds come in a certain direction it is very difficult for the dredge to do any amount of work per diem. In the fall of 1908 the weather became very severe.
They got 1,360 cubic yards in a day.

I do not know how much they did in a day; I can only say that during a great many days they were



unable to work at all. I know that from personal observation. What they 3id when the weather was good and when they could work is to me unknown, but I do know that time and again when I was in the vicinity, on account of the weather, the dredge was .unable to do any work whatever. She was compelled to go away from the scene of her work in November.

The hon. member's statement agrees very largely with that of the resident engineer who reported that the work would require to be continued, and he stated in his report last year that the work that had already been done was of such a character that it would fill up during the season of 1909.
I am not an expert on such matters, but it would be self-evident to me that this would occur at almost any place.

The statement of the engineer was that it would require to be continued last season. I understand from the hon. member for Westmorland that the work was not continued last season, and that the opening was not made in the channel.
Then my hon. friend misunderstood me. The work was continued last season, but too late to finish it up and on account of the inclemency of the weather they had to leave it.
How long did the dredge work last season?
I could not tell you. I was away in the United States during the time she was there.

The reason I ask is that I understood from the chief engineer of the department, in the course of his examination before the Public Accounts Committee, that the government dredge was not at work there, and did no work during the last season.
She certainly did.
And I understood the minister to say the other day that the government dredge was sent there, and prosecuted the work during 1909.

She did, and I know from a gentleman who was here recently who is veri? much interested, he being a citizen of Port Elgin, that the dredge had been there, and had done work during last autumn. I do not know of it personally, because I was absent from the country during the autumn months of last season.

The hon. gentleman must be mistaken as to what the chief engineer said. I cannot conceive it possible Mr. EMMERSON.
that he made that statement knowing that the dredge was sent there, and he tells me that he did not say such a thing. I made the statement myself that last year, owing to it becoming necessary, if we were to do this work at all, to do it by a government dredge, I tried to send a government dredge there as early as possible, but the government dredges were all engaged upon necessary work elsewhere, and it was not until late in the season that I was able to take a government dredge away from other wrork and sent her to Gaspereau. She went to Gaspereau and continued the work of dredging there until the season was so far advanced that it was necessary for her to leave the place, and go into winter quarters. In the coming season we propose to continue the work commenced on 1908, and which was continued last year in order to give access for vessels to Port Elgin. .

I certainly understood the chief engineer-and I do not intend to discuss the evidence which has been taken -to make the statement which I have repeated to the committee. I will be very much surprised if the minister does not find that statement in the concluding portion of the chief engineer's evidence where I asked him if the work was continued the following season by the government dredge, I referring at the same time to the statement that the minister had made in the House. He may have misunderstood me or I may have misunderstood him.
The hon. gentleman knows that I stated in the House that the government dredge had been sent there.
Yes.

The chief engineer tells me, that you may have misunderstood him, or,he did not understand your question, because he did not intend to say anything of the kind. The reports show the time she was there.
While the item of general dredging for the maritime provinces is under discussion, I wish to ask the minister whether he has decided that he can do any dredging at the port of Weymouth this year?

I am not able at this moment to -say when we shall be able to do the dredging work that will be required at Weymouth. What we intend to do, is to apportion the vote among the places which most urgently require dredging work.

At this point it may be desirable for me to give the minister some information respecting the needs of Weymouth. I brought this matter to the attention of the minister last year, and at that time there was no money available for the purpose, or "the arrangements had been

made for ihe dredging for the season, and consequently it was not convenient to take the matter up. At present, Weymouth is very much in need of some dredging at the entrance to the harbour, and also for the straightening of the channel up the river. Some time ago a plan of the river and harbour was made by the department's engineer, and it was intimated that certain dredging work would be undertaken before long. Up to the present time the department has not reached that work. I may say that very great inconvenience is experienced by shippers and others at this important commercial centre owing to the fact that it is very difficult to get the class of vessels that go to Weymouth over the bar and up the river at different times of the tide. At certain times also two steamers, which call at that port regularly, are obliged to lie off St. Mary's bay, because they cannot pass over the bar at the entrance to the river. I pointed out to the minister last year that Weymouth was an important commercial centre, the geographical centre of the county of Digby, and the centre of a large population; that a large lumbering business and a large pulp business were carried on in the immediate vicinity, and that the business of the port would be very considerably increased if the shipping facilities were improved by some dredging and some improvement of the harbour. As the vote this year is almost twice what it was last year, I hope that it will be possible for the minister to give some attention to the needs of Weymouth. It seems, from the report which has been brought down in reference to the dredges which are available for the Department of Public Works, that there are now no less than ten in use; and as three of these at least-and they seem to be dredges of greater capacity than those that have heretofore been used by the department- have been provided in the last four years, I hope that the minister, when he makes his arrangements with regard to the dredging in the maritime provinces, will be enabled to consider the needs of Weymouth.

I have given a good deal of consideration to the question of dredging at Weymouth, and, while I recognize that dredging is required there, as it is in many other places to which we are not able to give attention at the present time, yet the quantity of dredging required at Weymouth, to be effective and to give to the people what they are asking for is so large that I hesitate to recommend to my colleagues the undertaking of the work, at the present time at all events. If I remember rightly, the estimate of the chief engineer is that about 500,000 cubic yards will have to be removed. That is a very large amount of dredging; and, in view of this fact, I am not able to say with any definiteness to-152J
night, whether the work will be undertaken during the coming season, or just what decision will be arrived at with regard to it.

I may point out to the minister one fact in regard to Weymouth which may influence him a little in making his decision; that is, that for years, I think since confederation, there has not been a dollar of public money expended there for any harbour improvements, with the exception of a very small sum which was . spent at some little distance from Weymouth'1. I am not asking the minister to do all the work which the report he has before him states it is essential to do in order to bring that port up to the position it should occupy; but 1 submit that he might make a beginning. He might, for instance, do some work at the entrance to the harbour in connection with the bar which I have mentioned, which would afford considerable relief to shippers and to the operators of the two steamers which call regularly at the port. I do not ask that all the work which the plans show to be necessary should be carried to completion out of this vote or during the ensuing year; but I submit that some commencement should in all reason be undertaken during the year for which this vote will be available.

I would like to get some information from the minister in regard to some of the dredging that is going on in the province of New Brunswick. I would like to know how much money has been expended in dredging at Dalhousie, and how much it is estimated will be expended there out of this vote during the coming summer?

I cannot give my hon. friend to-night a statement of the dredging which has been done at Dalhousie. I did not suppose my hon. friend would ask for that, because the matter has been under investigation by the Committee of Public Accounts.
How much has been expended at Dalhousie since the close of the last fiscal year?
I have not that information to-night.
Also, when is it expected that the work of dredging at the public wharf and also at the ferry slip at Dalhousie will be completed?

A good deal of dredging work is to be done at Dalhousie, and how soon it will be completed will depend on the description of dredge tbjat will be used. If we had a large and powerful dredge the work would be done much more quickly than it can be with one of the small dredges. I am not able to give the

hon. gentleman the information to-night, but I should think that it would take the whole season and perhaps two seasons to complete the dredging at the railway wharf and public wharf.
Is the minister able to state the quantity of dredging required at the public wharf?
I have the information in the department, but not here.
I would like to have that information.
I shall be glad to get it for my hon. friend.
Does the minister propose to continue the dredging which was done at Digby last year?

There is more work to be done at Digby. I am not at the moment prepared to say whether we will continue it during the present season or not. I will look into the reports and determine whether it is urgently required or not? Of course, we cannot engage in all dredging work at once, and we have to take first the places where dredging is most urgently required.
The plans will disclose that they have not been worked up to.
No, there is still work to be done under the plans.

To show the urgency of the need for this work I would say that an arrangement has been made with one of the steamship companies plying between the United States and Nova Scotia to run a direct boat from Boston to Digby beginning on the 1st of July. That boat will" require more wharf and harbour accommodation than is required by the boats plying between St. John and Digby. The operating of this new service will be of importance and benefit to all of Nova Scotia, and aDo to the province of New Brunswick, which is sharing very largely in that profitable summer business. Then, the fishing interests in Digby, along with some others in different parts of Nova Scotia, are being, I am informed, amalgamated, and when that amalgamation is completed, I understand considerable additions will be made to the plant, and a much increased business in this line will be done in Digby. A reasonable amount of dredging in one part of the harbour would undoubtedly afford this Boston steamer increased accommodation, and would also afford better facilities for the larger fishing business which it is likely will be carried on by the fleet.

When we come to apportion the amount the question of continuing the dredging at Digby during the pre-Mr. PUGSLEY.
sent season will be carefully considered. Referring to Dalhousie, during the season of 1909, the A. and R. Loggie dredge ' Reliable ', afterwards named the ' Invader ', worked in the ferry business at Dalhousie, dredging about the pier head, and the new ferry wharf berths for schooners with thirteen feet of water, and next the Dalhousie wharf a berth for deep water vessels seventy-five feet wide six hundred feet long, and twenty feet deep at low water. The material removed was 62,735 cubic yards, costing $31,632.
Is the work at the wharf of the Dalhousie Lumber company completed?

It is completed to the depth of fifteen feet, but the traffic coming to the wharf requires a depth of twenty-one feet. It is for us to consider whether we will go on dredging to a depth of twenty-one feet or not.
How much was expended last year upon that?
30,546 cubic yards were removed since the close of the last fiscal year.
Was any work done at Caraquet last year?
Yes, dredging operations were performed across the shoal in Caraquet harbour. 48,772 cubic yards were removed.
Is that to be continued during the coming season?
We have not decided as to that; there is necessity for completing the work.
When contracts are let do they specify the depth to which the dredging is to be done, or the quantity that is to be removed?

Sometimes they have in the past and sometimes not. We think it is the better practice to determine the depth to which the dredging shall be carried on and specify it' in the specifications. I think the coming year we will do it in all cases.
At Caraquet I judge the depth was not specified.
That is a matter for the resident engineer. He lays out the work and the dredge is supposed to work according to his direction.

This seems a very objectionable practice in the letting of contracts. At Dalhousie, for instance, I understand the contract was simply a contract to do dredging at Dalhousie without specifying where. The' contract wras let to

a contractor, and the work might go on from year to year for ten years, or as long as the resident engineer could find anything to dredge at any point in the harbour. In the case of Dalhousie, from the documents brought down, the contemplation of the department at the start seems to have been that the dredging should be done at the public wharf. The dredge was removed, after a few weeks work, from that to another point, where I do not believe any work was contem plated at the time the contract was let. They go on working her the greater part of the season, then they go on the next season at the same place, and the minister tells us the work is going on next year and has no idea where it is going to stop. This is a most reckless way of letting contracts involving such immense sums. The same remark is true with regard to Loggieville, and other places where dredging is being done. A contract is let and one has not the slightest conception how many years it is to continue. It is all done as the resident engineer may direct. He may direct dredging to be done and to be continued to a depth as in the case of Loggieville, of 15 feet. Then the department determines to carry it another season to 20 feet, and that contract goes on, and the government seems helpless. The practice is most objectionable. If the minister had any regard for the proper conduct of his business, he would introduce some new regulations which would provide for contracts that had some definiteness, and the department would have some idea when they would come to an end. At present A. & R. Loggie, and other firms in New Brunswick have contracts for dredging that may be continued for years to come.

The hon. gentleman either forgets the facts or he does not think it worth while to state them. Ever since the department has been doing dredging work the practice has been, in the great majority of cases, to let contracts for dredging at certain points. The resident engineer is on the spot. He knows better whether it is best to make one cut right up to the wharfs or two cuts, depending on whether it is possible to give accommodation by making the one or the two cuts, or giving a lesser depth first and making the cut right up to the wharf and later on digging to a greater depth. The practice has been to let contracts for dredging at certain places without actually attempting to lay out the work definitely, to do which would require a great deal of survey work in order to have any accuracy. The hon. gentleman says that the Loggie contract may go on for years, and that the other contracts may do the same. According to my recollection, the contract of the Messrs.
Loggie is for the season of navigation, or such further period as the minister may determine. Therefore, unless the minister extends the contract, the Messrs. Loggie or others will only be entitled to- dredge for that season. As regards extending a contract, the minister would naturally consult his engineering staff, and from the plan made by the resident engineer he would see how much dredging had actually been done, what depth of water there was in the harbour, and what accommodation to shipping, and whether it was reasonably necessary to continue the work. By all these things he would be influenced in determining whether or not the contract would be extended. As regards Dalhousie harbour, a contract was let for the work.
Without specifying any particular part.

Yes, where necessary to accommodate the people, and the layout of the work was done entirely by the resident engineer. Some remarks have been made by the hon. gentleman as to work being done at certain points. With that the minister has nothing to do. That was purely determined by the engineering department, especially the resident engineer. The resident engineer would be guided by the interests of the port and would have the work done wheie it would best accommodate the pressing necessities of business, and the layout of the work would rest entirely with the resident engineer Neither the minister nor any of the officials of the department interfere at all with him in the exercise of his judgment.

The minister has said that I either forgot the facts or deliberately refrained from mentioning them. But no one who has listened to his statement could have failed to observe that he himself mentioned no fact whatever which I had not mentioned myself.
Did not the hon. gentle* man say that the Messrs. Loggie had a contract which they could hold the Crown to-for ten years?

I said they had a contract which might go on from year to year for ten years, and which has gone on, in the case of the dredging at Loggieville and Dalhousie, for three years and apparently, according to the minister's statement, is intended to be continued the coming season at least.	,

The hon. gentleman is wrong. There was only one extension of the contract at Loggieville. They were tenderers in the different years and they received the contract in the ordinary way, and after that there was but one extension.

I refer to the dredging given them in the season of 1908, and which

the minister said had been continued last year, and they got some three years in all.
That was only one extension, and the hon. gentleman said it had been extended fpr three years.
I said in the case of the dredging at Dalhousie there was a contract two years and the minister announced it was to be extended next year.
I did not.
Then I certainly misunderstood him. Did he not state the dredging was to continue next year?
The hon. gentleman wishes to draw the inference that I said the Loggie contract was to be continued another year. I made no such statement, and no decision has been arrived at on the subject.
Can he not state whether the Messrs. Loggie will continue the dredging at Dalhousie next season?
The matter has not been considered at all.
But the work not completed, which was let them by contract in 1908, was continued by them last year?
Yes.
The minister states that, according to his recollection, there is a clause in the contract which limited the dredging to the season of navigation.
And which may be extended further as the minister may see fit.

I would not care to speak from memory as to whether in these particular contracts there is such a term. I know there are some which are thus limited, and the contents are sometimes required by order in council to be so limited.
I feel quite sure such a limit is in this, but I am not quite positive.

That does not alter the case if the minister, as a matter of course, does renew the contracts from year to year. If it be the case that the contract is limited to the season of 1908, did he call for further tenders in 1909?
The hon. gentleman has already been informed that I did not.

So it amounts to precisely the same thing, whether the term is in the contract or not. Contracts are let for dredging in a harbour without designating the wharf or the localities where the dredging is to be done, and it is only one who is able to get information either from .the resident engineer or the officers of the department, who is in a position to tender. That is one

thing which is very objectionable. Tenders are called for without giving any information whatever upon which contractors could base a tender. It is necessary, before a contractor can put in a proper tender, or estimate what the work is likely to cost, to ascertain where the dredging is to be done.
Which he always can do.
That may or may not be.
And more than that, w'hen the contractor puts in his tender, he must state that he has acquired information as to the dredging.

Nevertheless there are cases where intending tenderers have not been able to obtain that information. I have not introduced this discussion for the purpose of raising matters that have been under investigation in the Public Accounts Committee, but to call attention to what seems to me a very loose method in awarding these contracts, a method that leaves the door wide open for all sorts of conduct which, I think, would not be thought to be in the public interest. I think that, in connection with this matter, there c light to be some requirement that, when a contract is let, the department itself and the public ought to know just what is expected to be done, and not leave it open to what the minister says has occurred in the ports of Dalhousie and Loggieville-a contract made for one season and continued from year to year so long as the department can find anything to be done in the vicinity of the particular point which is named in the contract.

No need of keeping the item for that-

Not for that particularly. I think we are not called upon to pass this item with the meagre information which the minister has communicated to the House to-night. There are many places the minister has mentioned in which these moneys are to be expended. For my part, I wish to know, first, whether, where the dredging is to be done during the next season, and I want, at this time and before the item passes, to attempt to discover just what reports have been made as to the necessity of dredging at these places, what examination has been made and what reports received, and what the estimated expenditure of the dredging is. I say to the minister, quite frankly, that I want information with regard to the places that he has named in which dredging is to be done, and this information I am entitled to as a member of this com
mittee. As far as I am concerned,I certainly do press the request I made that the item should stand until the information is given to the committee.

I would like to know, with reference to the dredging at Bathurst, just what it is proposed to do there. What expenditure was made at Bathurst last year?

So far as future work is concerned, we have not decided concerning Bathurst. We want a full report as to Bathurst. We did) [DOT]considerable at Bathurst last year. There appear to have been 272,00 cubic yards removed last year both from the harbour and from the bar.

48C0
Mr. CROCKET, tors at Bathurst?
Who were the contrac-

Messrs A. & R. Loggie.

I have not these particulars with me to-night.
I would like to have the information.
I shall be glad to give the information later.

I would like to know if tenders were called for.
Mr. PUGSLEY, I will get the information.

Some 72,UUO.

I think the members of this House are entitled to know where it is proposed to expend this $675,000 which is appropriated for dredging in the maritime provinces. Loggie, under the same arrangement they had with the Department of Public Works for doing last season's work?

We are considering doing considerable dredging at Bathurst, necessitated by the development of the iron deposits some eighteen miles from Bathurst. The company have in contemplation, if the harbour can be improved, the shipment of a large quantity of their ore from Bathurst, and also the establishment of smelting works there. But until a report is received showing the character of the soil, and the quantity of material to be dredged, and until we make up our minds as to what it is going to cost, we will not be able .to come to a decision. Borings are now being made by one of the engineers of the department, through the ice. We expect these reports in shortly, and then the matter will be taken up and considered.
I would like the information as to whether tenders were called for, and if so, when they were called for, what tenders were received, and the prices offered.
I think it is now about time to adjourn. This is an item that will provoke a good deal of discussion.
I think we had better finish up this item.
I will be happy to give my hon. friend the information later.
What was the price?
$3 per cubic yard for rock, and 41 cents for loose material.
Was that material all towed to the dumping ground, or was it cast over as in the previous year?
I have not the information, but I will be glad to get it.

I have not said so.
Well is it, or is it not?

engineer is now completing his work of survey.

I would like to know exactly where the work was done last season.

Part of it was done in removing a sharp bend in the channel at the approach to the public wharf and increasing the depth in the berth at the public wharf. Then there was a quantity of material removed to give passage for logs at low water near the Bathurst Lumber Company's mill. A quantity of material was removed from the ballast bar and also a auantitv of mud from what is known as the Tetegouche bar at a point in the channel leading to Bathurst harbour. Of course, all that will ibe useful work in connection with the carrying out of the larger scheme.
Is this amount to be expended under contract or does it include any amount to be expended on government dredges as well?
We will require about $250,000 to, operate the government dredges and that will leave available $425,000 for contract work.

I was not here when this item was first called up, but as a matter of fact, most of the principal items in dredging: are looked after in the Estimates by special appropriations.
